assessment_summary: The statement is false. The greedy algorithm does not always return a minimum vertex cover. A counterexample can be constructed where a suboptimal vertex has a higher degree than the vertices forming the optimal cover.
counterexample: Consider a graph with vertices V = {x, a1, a2, a3, y1, y2, y3} and edges E = {(x, a1), (x, a2), (x, a3), (a1, y1), (a2, y2), (a3, y3)}. The optimal minimum vertex cover is {a1, a2, a3} with size 3. However, the greedy algorithm will initially select vertex x, because it uniquely has the maximum degree (3, while a1, a2, a3 have degree 2). After removing x and its incident edges, the remaining edges are exactly (a1, y1), (a2, y2), and (a3, y3), which are completely disjoint. The greedy algorithm will need to pick 3 additional vertices (one for each of these edges), resulting in a vertex cover of size 4 (e.g., {x, a1, a2, a3}). Since 4 > 3, the greedy algorithm fails to return a minimum vertex cover.
